analysis.one_liner: Gives age and race discrimination victims the same damages that sex discrimination victims already get.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or vote; it died in committee when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal civil rights law already lets workers who win sex discrimination cases recover compensatory and punitive damages and get a jury trial. Workers who win race or national origin discrimination cases, and older workers under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, do not get the full set of those remedies. This bill would have made the remedies equal for all of them. It was referred to two House committees and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who experience race, color, national origin, religious, or age discrimination and sue their employers, who could recover compensatory and punitive damages and get jury trials on par with sex discrimination claims.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers facing race or age discrimination

how_it_helps.text: Extends compensatory and punitive damages to all victims of intentional race, color, religion, and national origin discrimination in employment, equalizing remedies across Title VII bases [S2].
Adds jury trial rights for all parties in these civil rights damages cases [S2].
Amends the Age Discrimination in Employment Act to provide the same legal and equitable relief as Title VII, including compensatory and punitive damages for older workers [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers found liable for age or race discrimination would face larger damage awards and jury trials; defendants in these cases would also have guaranteed jury trial rights.

drawbacks.text: Removing the ADEA's traditional remedies structure could create new litigation exposure for employers of older workers, including higher jury awards.
Small businesses could face higher settlement costs in discrimination cases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is fair, equal remedies for workers regardless of which protected characteristic was targeted, at a modest cost to employers in meritorious cases. The bill was narrow and focused, though it died without any committee action.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and no committee ever acted on it before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced May 8, 2024 and referred jointly to the Education and Workforce and Judiciary committees [S4].
No hearings, markups, or floor votes ever occurred [S4].
The Congress ended January 3, 2025, killing the bill [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers facing age or race discrimination claims gained the most, since the bill that would have expanded damages against them died without a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republicans supported it, and no committee or floor action followed.

industries.note: Would face expanded compensatory and punitive damages and jury trials in race and age discrimination cases.
